overview: This file assembles State Department reporting on Japanese newspaper opinion from the opening months of the Allied occupation through the end of 1949, together with one charge slip and several reports concerning wider Asian and European affairs. The early telegrams summarize editorials on hunger, economic democratization, labor and land reform, the Shidehara government, popular sovereignty, the imperial institution, war responsibility, and the purge of militarists. Later documents trace Japanese reactions to communism, China policy, Soviet detention of Japanese prisoners, economic decontrol, the peace treaty and territorial questions, while also preserving interviews and commentary by Shigeru Yoshida, Tao Hsi-sheng, and Amiya C. Chakravarty.

subfiles.title: Japanese press comment, November 6–12, 1945
subfiles.about: A weekly survey of Japanese editorials concerning food, economic democratization, government, political parties, agriculture, and labor.
subfiles.summary: The telegram emphasizes the severe food and shipping crises and newspapers' demands for price controls, imports, improved distribution, and land reclamation. Editorials welcome the dissolution of the zaibatsu but argue that deeper economic democratization is necessary. The Shidehara government, Liberal Party, former Japan Political Association members, police, civil service, landlords, and insufficiently organized labor all receive criticism.

subfiles.title: Japanese press comment, November 20–26, 1945
subfiles.about: A press survey covering public morale, the Diet, production, land and labor reform, financial policy, and war guilt.
subfiles.summary: Japanese editorials describe low morale and political passivity while warning against both isolation and uncritical imitation of the West. They criticize the existing Diet and government, urge food imports and increased coal and industrial production, and debate land and trade-union bills. The survey concludes with demands that Japanese authorities investigate war crimes and remove compromised officials without waiting for SCAP action.

subfiles.title: Japanese editorial comment, November 26–December 4, 1945
subfiles.about: A detailed digest of editorials on the Shidehara government, democracy, political parties, economic production, taxation, and war responsibility.
subfiles.summary: The press faults Shidehara's Diet address and his cabinet's lack of initiative while discussing popular sovereignty and the compatibility of democracy with the imperial institution. Newspapers also address elections, party financing, foreign trade, the coal crisis, wartime-profit and property taxes, and the risk of deflation. Editorials demand investigation of the causes of war, identify Tojo and Konoe with war responsibility, and welcome SCAP's arrest of fifty-nine alleged war criminals.

subfiles.title: Telegram on emerging democratic and antiwar opinion
subfiles.about: An assessment of Japanese press criticism of the emperor, wartime leadership, and the government's failure to pursue war criminals.
subfiles.summary: The telegram detects a growing body of opinion willing to support occupation reforms and critically reconsider Japan's political structure and wartime conduct. It notes unprecedented public discussion of the imperial institution, including demands for Hirohito's abdication and a Communist newspaper's caricature of the emperor. Pearl Harbor anniversary editorials demand investigation and punishment of war leaders, although Atcheson cautions that these views may not yet represent settled public opinion.

subfiles.title: Central-files charge slip
subfiles.about: A record of two charged-out telegram enclosures associated with the file.
subfiles.summary: The slip records a February 17, 1945 enclosure concerning telegram no. 120 from Bucharest as charged to PED–Suppsmyer on April 20, 1945. It also records a December 29, 1945 enclosure concerning telegram no. 226 from Tokyo as charged to Ken Lee on January 24, 1946.

subfiles.title: Japanese press comment, February 6–12, 1946
subfiles.about: A press survey focused on the political purge, inflation, elections, labor disputes, trade revival, and the Yamashita trial.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers speculate about the electoral effects of the January 4 purge directives and criticize the Shidehara cabinet's labor, constitutional, and anti-inflation policies. They debate the quality of Diet candidates, the need for a broader political purge, and prospects for a popular front. Economic commentary stresses production, consumer unions, cotton exports, corporate reorganization, and workers' participation, while reports on the Yamashita trial emphasize both the enormity of the crimes and procedural fairness.

subfiles.title: Japanese press reaction to the French political crisis
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, GHQ SCAP, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Department of the Army, for Department of State information
subfiles.about: A report on Japanese newspaper interpretations of strikes, communism, and political conflict in France and Italy.
subfiles.summary: Yomiuri attributes the French strike crisis to Communist control of organized labor and support among farmers, while a Sendai paper interprets the conflict through French capitalism, administrative weakness, and distrust of dictatorship. A Niigata-area paper treats events in France and Italy as part of intensifying American-Soviet competition. It argues that the Marshall Plan might weaken Soviet control in Eastern Europe but intensify Communist offensives in Western Europe.

subfiles.title: Tao Hsi-sheng on the U.S. China White Paper
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington; repeated to Embassy Office, Canton
subfiles.about: A report on Tao Hsi-sheng's criticism of the U.S. China White Paper and American policy toward the Chinese Civil War.
subfiles.summary: Tao calls the White Paper an alibi for a failed wait-and-see policy and argues that Washington misunderstood Chinese Communism as an agrarian reform movement rather than part of the Soviet-led Communist International. Although he accepts the document's criticisms of the Nationalist Party and government, he contends that China requires immediate military assistance and a new, positive American policy.

subfiles.title: United Press interview with Prime Minister Yoshida
subfiles.about: An airgram reproducing Shigeru Yoshida's remarks on the peace treaty, occupation, China, communism, war, taxation, and reconstruction.
subfiles.summary: Yoshida favors an early peace treaty but doubts that U.S. occupation forces can withdraw rapidly without leaving Japan vulnerable and disorderly. He advises foreign powers to leave China alone, faults Chiang Kai-shek's government for inadequate reforms, and predicts that Chinese Communism will influence Japan only gradually. He also discusses avoiding another world war, balancing Japan's austerity budget, attracting foreign capital, and Japanese gratitude for American food aid and MacArthur's leadership.

subfiles.title: Chakravarty interview on India, Japan, and the Bangkok conference
subfiles.about: A report on a Nippon Times article concerning Amiya C. Chakravarty's expectations for Indian and Japanese roles in Asian development and anticommunism.
subfiles.summary: The article predicts that the Bangkok conference may combine India's moral influence with Japanese technical capacity in developing Asian countries. Chakravarty links Philip Jessup's planned call on SCAP to the favorable American reception of Nehru's tour. William Draper's discussions with Nehru and visit to Japan are presented as further evidence that India and Japan may receive major regional roles in opposition to communism.

subfiles.title: Japanese press summary, December 16–22, 1949
subfiles.about: A weekly press summary covering Soviet repatriation, Mao's Moscow visit, public-sector wages, Formosa, territorial questions, and German security.
subfiles.summary: The press gives extensive attention to the Allied Council confrontation over Japanese still detained or unaccounted for in Soviet territory and condemns the Soviet member's walkout. Mao Zedong's visit to Moscow is interpreted as heralding closer Sino-Soviet relations and a possible new treaty. Domestic coverage concentrates on the Yoshida cabinet's struggle over year-end bonuses and wage increases, while foreign-affairs reporting shows interest in Formosa and the possible return of the Kurils, Habomai, Shikotan, Okinawa, the Bonins, and Iwo Jima.

subfiles.title: Japanese press reactions at the end of December 1949
subfiles.about: A weekly survey of Japanese coverage of Soviet-held prisoners, economic decontrol, war-criminal amnesty, party realignment, territorial claims, and Philippine hostility.
subfiles.summary: Coverage of the repatriation dispute links MacArthur's proposed neutral investigation with the Khabarovsk germ-warfare trial, which non-Communist papers treat skeptically. Newspapers welcome commodity and trade decontrol but caution that Japan must compete responsibly in world markets; they also report MacArthur's amnesty for forty-six minor war criminals. Political reporting considers Ken Inukai's prospective move into Yoshida's party, while foreign-policy commentary highlights the peace treaty, Japanese claims to neighboring islands, and Philippine resentment of Japan.

interest: The file provides an unusually concentrated record of how occupation officials selected, condensed, and interpreted Japanese editorial opinion during a period of rapid political change. It captures public discussion of subjects that had recently been dangerous or impossible to print—including imperial responsibility, popular sovereignty, war crimes, labor organization, and criticism of senior statesmen. The later reports are especially useful for tracing Japan's movement from immediate postwar survival toward Cold War questions of communism, China, Soviet repatriation, economic independence, a peace treaty, and the recovery of disputed islands.
